title: Central-isogeny lifting and adjoint-torus ambiguity over arbitrary rings
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring. Let $(G_i,T_i=D_A(M_i))$, $i=0,1$, be split realizations in the sense of [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization], with reduced root data $(M_i,\Phi_i,M_i^\vee,\Phi_i^\vee)$; no bases or pinning generators are specified. Suppose $h:M_0\hookrightarrow M_1$ is an injective homomorphism with finite cokernel and $b:\Phi_1\to\Phi_0$ is a bijection satisfying
$$h(b(\alpha))=\alpha,\qquad h^\vee(\alpha^\vee)=b(\alpha)^\vee\quad(\alpha\in\Phi_1).$$
Here $h^\vee$ is restriction of integer-valued functionals. There exists a homomorphism $f:G_1\to G_0$ whose restriction to $T_1$ is the specified constant monomial map $D_A(h):T_1\to T_0$ [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. It is finite, faithfully flat and finitely presented, with central scheme-theoretic kernel $D_A(M_1/h(M_0))\subseteq T_1$. Finite means affine with finite coordinate module over the target; faithfully flat means flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] and surjective. In particular, when $h$ is an isomorphism, $f$ is an isomorphism. The tangent map of every such $f$ restricts to an $A$-module isomorphism $\mathfrak g_{1,\alpha}\simeq\mathfrak g_{0,b(\alpha)}$ for each root. For any two such homomorphisms $f,F$ inducing the same $h,b$, there exists a unique $t\in(T_0/Z(G_0))(A)$ with $F=c_t\circ f$, where $c_t$ is the action on $G_0$ descended from conjugation. Here $Z(G_0)$ is the subgroup functor commuting with every point after every algebra extension, and $T_0/Z(G_0)$ denotes the fppf sheaf quotient (sheafification of the pointwise quotient for flat finitely presented jointly surjective covers). These statements allow disconnected and nonreduced $A$, empty roots, and rank zero; the kernel need not be smooth.

source.place: Theorem 6.1.16(1), printed p.196, proved in Section 6.2, pp.204--210, restricted to root exponents one; Definition 6.1.8 and Example 6.1.9, p.191; Lemma 6.1.4, pp.187--189; Corollary 6.1.15, pp.195--196; Proposition 3.3.10, p.103. Read online; local PDF WANTED. No Stacks tag states this group-scheme isogeny theorem.

proof.text: Choose a base $\Delta_1$ using [lem-sfb-small-centralizer-hom-amalgamation]. Since $h$ has finite cokernel, $h_{\mathbf Q}$ is an isomorphism, and $h(b(\alpha))=\alpha$ shows that $\Delta_0=b(\Delta_1)$ is rationally independent and gives the same signed integral expansions of all roots. Thus it is a base by [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Choose generators of the finitely many simple-root modules on both sides. For $J\subseteq\Delta_1$, form the centralizers $G_{1,J}$ and $G_{0,b(J)}$ of [lem-sfb-small-centralizer-hom-amalgamation]. They retain the full tori, their root modules and the inherited generators. Their root sets are matched by $b$, since $h_{\mathbf Q}$ identifies the rational spans, and the original coroot equality still holds. For $|J|\leq2$, [lem-sfb-low-rank-pinned-root-hom] gives normalized maps $g_J:G_{1,J}\to G_{0,b(J)}$ with torus restriction $D_A(h)$. Its restriction clause gives $g_J|_{G_{1,I}}=g_I$ for $I\subseteq J$. Compose each with $G_{0,b(J)}\hookrightarrow G_0$ and apply the amalgamation assertion to obtain $f:G_1\to G_0$. Its restriction to $G_{1,\varnothing}=T_1$ is exactly $D_A(h)$. The empty-base case uses $G_i=T_i$ and just this monomial map.

source.place: Proof of Isogeny Theorem, Step 1, printed pp.204--205; Corollary 6.2.7; Example 6.2.6 and Lemma 6.2.8 for its low-rank inputs.

proof.text: In fact take any homomorphism $g:G_1\to G_0$ with the specified torus restriction and lattice data. At every algebraically closed $A$-field $\Omega$, [lem-sfb-root-monomial-kernel-coordinates] applies to $g_\Omega$, with every root exponent $q_\alpha=1$. It gives surjectivity and a finite kernel whose open-cell coordinates have all additive factors trivial: the kernel is exactly $\ker(D_\Omega(h))$ inside $T_{1,\Omega}$. Every source root is $h(b(\alpha))$, so every source root character is trivial on that torus kernel. Consequently it lies in $D_\Omega(M_1/\mathbf Z\Phi_1)=Z(G_{1,\Omega})$ by [lem-sfb-adjoint-torus-root-coordinates]. Thus all geometric fibres of $g$ have finite central kernel. Apply [lem-sfb-fibral-central-isogeny-recognition] to conclude that $g$, in particular the map constructed in step 1, is finite, flat, surjective and finitely presented, with central kernel. This uses fibrewise recognition over arbitrary $A$, rather than inferring a scheme-theoretic equality merely from agreement on geometric points.

The central kernel $K$ is contained in $Z(G_1)\subseteq T_1$ by [lem-sfb-adjoint-torus-root-coordinates]. Hence $K=\ker(g|_{T_1})$ scheme-theoretically: on every algebra, an element of the latter kernel is killed by $g$, while every element killed by $g$ lies in $T_1$. The kernel formula in [lem-sfb-relative-diagonalizable-character-duality] now gives $K=D_A(M_1/h(M_0))$ with precisely the indicated embedding. If $h$ is an isomorphism, $K=1$. The quotient description of [lem-sfb-fibral-central-isogeny-recognition] then identifies $G_1\times_{G_0}G_1$ with $G_1\times_A1$, and its projection to $G_1$ is an isomorphism. This projection is the pullback of $g$ along $g$, a finite faithfully flat, hence quasi-compact, cover. Isomorphism descent [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-descend-isomorphism] therefore makes $g$ an isomorphism.

source.place: Example 6.1.9, printed pp.191--192; Appendix B.1; Proposition 3.3.10 and the preceding fppf quotient discussion; Stacks Tag 02L4 (descent of isomorphisms).

proof.text: By step 2 every homomorphism in question is a quasi-finite surjection. Apply [lem-sfb-quasifinite-root-map-rigidity]: in chosen generators its differential on each root module is multiplication by a unit $a_\alpha$. Multiplication by $a_\alpha^{-1}$ is the inverse, proving the asserted tangent isomorphisms. For two such maps $f,F$, retain the bases and simple-root generators of step 1 and write $df(X_{1,\alpha})=a_\beta X_{0,\beta}$ and $dF(X_{1,\alpha})=A_\beta X_{0,\beta}$, where $\beta=b(\alpha)$. Set $r_\beta=A_\beta a_\beta^{-1}$. Since $\Delta_0$ is a base, $Q_0=\mathbf Z\Phi_0=\bigoplus_{\beta\in\Delta_0}\mathbf Z\beta$: signed integral expansions give spanning, and rational independence gives integral independence. The formula $t(\sum n_\beta\beta)=\prod r_\beta^{n_\beta}$ defines a unique homomorphism $Q_0\to A^\times$. By [lem-sfb-adjoint-torus-root-coordinates] it gives $t\in(T_0/Z(G_0))(A)$, and $c_t$ fixes $T_0$ and multiplies the $\beta$-root module by $r_\beta$. Thus $d(c_t\circ f)(X_{1,\alpha})=r_\beta a_\beta X_{0,\beta}=A_\beta X_{0,\beta}$. The two maps also have the same torus restriction, so pinning rigidity gives $F=c_t\circ f$.

source.place: Lemma 6.1.4, pp.188--189; Proposition 6.1.13(2), pp.194--195; proof of Corollary 6.1.15, pp.195--196.

proof.text: If another $s\in(T_0/Z(G_0))(A)$ satisfies $F=c_s\circ f$, then [lem-sfb-adjoint-torus-root-coordinates] gives $s(\beta)a_\beta=A_\beta$ for every simple root. As each $a_\beta$ is a unit, $s(\beta)=r_\beta=t(\beta)$, and the basis of $Q_0$ in step 4 forces $s=t$. All these are identities over the whole ring and on all algebra extensions. For empty roots, $Q_0=0$ and the conjugating torus is trivial; for rank zero both groups are trivial. None of the arguments inverts the order of the finite lattice cokernel; for example the power map on $\mathbf G_m$ can have kernel $\mu_p$ in characteristic $p$, which is allowed.

source.place: Proof of Corollary 6.1.15, printed pp.195--196; empty-root specialization.
